meta.description: What could Chicago’s quantum campus mean for South Side residents? Explore jobs, housing, environmental questions and practical ways to participate.

hero.eyebrow: South Chicago · South Shore · East Side
hero.headlineFuture: What does it mean for your neighborhood?
hero.subhead: The Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP) is being developed at the former U.S. Steel South Works site in South Chicago. It could bring jobs, businesses and learning opportunities — alongside questions about housing costs, the environment and who benefits.
hero.trustNote: Free to use. No account needed, and we never ask for your real name.

timeline.title: Every revolution changed Chicago. Not everyone shared the gains.
timeline.intro: Here are five turning points. For each one, ask two questions: who gained, and who got left out?

stops.name: Railroads
stops.plain: Trains tied Chicago to the rest of the country.
stops.gained: Chicago became a huge railroad center with many jobs, and in 1937 the Pullman porters' union won the first major contract for a Black union.
stops.leftOut: Potawatomi and other Native nations were removed after an 1833 treaty, and Black Pullman porters (sleeping-car attendants) were kept in service jobs.

stops.name: Steel and heavy industry
stops.plain: Giant mills turned iron ore into steel.
stops.gained: Mills in South Chicago and nearby neighborhoods gave thousands of families steady work for about a century.
stops.leftOut: Many Black workers were passed over for promotions, yet steel paid for homes and college, and when the mills closed, whole neighborhoods lost those paychecks.

stops.name: The internet
stops.plain: Computers and phones got connected to each other.
stops.gained: Easy web browsers like Mosaic spread, and Chicago Connected later gave many CPS families free internet at home for learning.
stops.leftOut: Not everyone got online. In 2020, an estimated 100,000 Chicago students still lacked high-speed internet at home.

stops.name: Artificial intelligence (AI)
stops.plain: Software that learns patterns from examples.
stops.gained: Workers and companies that use AI tools gain new options, and a degree or more job training can help lower the risk of automation.
stops.leftOut: A Chicago Fed study of U.S. jobs found Black workers make up more than their share of 17 of the 30 jobs most likely to be automated (done by machines).

stops.name: Quantum technology
stops.plain: Computers built on the rules of very tiny things.
stops.gained: Illinois broke ground in September 2025 on a quantum technology park at the old South Works steel site, where steelmaking ended in 1992.
stops.leftOut: This time, jobs, training and a voice in the plan must reach neighbors in South Chicago. Planners say they are talking with City Colleges of Chicago about training and funding a neighborhood plan for South Chicago.

explainer.title: What is quantum, in 30 seconds?

steps.title: Bits
steps.text: Your phone and laptop store everything as bits. A bit is like a tiny switch that is either 0 or 1.

steps.title: Qubits
steps.text: A qubit is the quantum version of a bit. Until you measure it, it can be in a blend of 0 and 1. When you measure it, you always get a plain 0 or 1.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.text: Special programs can use that blend to help with a few hard problems, like studying how molecules behave.

explainer.notText: A quantum computer does not try every answer at once, and it will not replace your laptop. Today's machines are still small and make errors.

community.title: How could the quantum campus affect your community?
community.intro: What matters most to you? Choose a topic to open practical next steps. You do not need to understand the science to have a voice.
community.context: Confirmed: IQMP is being developed at South Works. Jobs and neighborhood benefits are expected, not guaranteed. The concerns below describe possible impacts, not proof that the campus has caused them.

topics.title: Housing costs & staying in your neighborhood
topics.issue: New investment could raise nearby rents, home prices or property taxes. The size of any campus-related change is uncertain.
topics.why: Longtime neighbors should be able to stay and share in new investment.
topics.today: Check your tenant rights and available rental assistance. Ask local representatives how housing protections will be tracked.
topics.proposal: Community advocates are seeking affordable housing and protections against displacement. New policies require action by government or developers.

topics.title: Jobs & career opportunities
topics.issue: The campus is expected to need construction and permanent workers, including technicians, logistics, security and office staff. These are potential roles, not current job listings.
topics.why: You may have useful skills already. Different roles require different training; a physics PhD is not the only route.
topics.today: Try our career matching quiz, then compare the skills, education and training resources on each career card. Check program costs, eligibility and application dates with the provider.
topics.proposal: Ask employers and training providers for accessible training and clear local hiring goals. Hiring and training commitments must come from those organizations.

topics.title: Environmental safety
topics.issue: South Works is a former industrial site. Illinois EPA publishes site investigations and cleanup documents; residents are asking about soil, construction dust, and future water and electricity use.
topics.why: Neighbors need clear information about how construction and operations could affect health and everyday life.
topics.today: Read the EPA site updates and contact information. Use them to ask about dust controls, cleanup progress and how to report a concern.
topics.proposal: Community groups are calling for transparent environmental monitoring. Published plans do not establish that every risk has been eliminated.

topics.title: Local businesses & everyday services
topics.issue: New workers and investment could bring customers. Existing shops may still face barriers to contracts, higher costs or unmet neighborhood needs.
topics.why: Growth should help local shops and improve access to groceries, pharmacies and transportation.
topics.today: Support neighborhood shops. Business owners can ask Center for Changing Lives about its South Chicago business advising and licensing support.
topics.proposal: Ask project leaders how existing businesses can access purchasing opportunities and how plans will address essential services. These improvements are not guaranteed.

topics.title: Community voice & transparency
topics.issue: Residents and community groups are seeking a binding community benefits agreement: a contract spelling out what a developer must deliver to neighbors.
topics.why: People in South Chicago, South Shore and East Side deserve a say in changes around them.
topics.today: Use IQMP’s community page for updates and ways to share questions. Ask who is responsible for commitments, when they are due and where progress will be published.
topics.proposal: Community groups are advocating for local hiring, housing and environmental protections. Their campaign is a request for commitments, not proof those protections are in place.

community.closing: Chicago’s quantum future should create opportunities for the communities that call the South Side home.
